patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Wilson is a 58-year-old man with severe chronic alcohol use disorder who is brought by ambulance in active status epilepticus. His neighbor, who checks on him regularly, called 911 when she found him convulsing on his front porch. She estimates she last saw him drinking 36 hours ago and that he had been trying to quit drinking this week after a conversation with his brother. He had no prior diagnosed epilepsy. He arrived by ambulance with continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity for approximately 20 minutes. Paramedics noted multiple old bruises from probable falls. No IV access was obtained by EMS due to poor venous access — midazolam 10 mg IM was given without termination of seizures. He is a chronic heavy drinker with 10+ drinks daily for 20 years. The abrupt cessation 36 hours prior is classic for alcohol withdrawal seizures and status epilepticus. The 24-72 hour window is the highest risk period for alcohol withdrawal seizures, and withdrawal SE is a medical emergency. He is malnourished with suspected thiamine deficiency. He has no prior epilepsy history — these are withdrawal seizures, not primary epilepsy. The key distinction is that alcohol withdrawal SE is from central nervous system hyperexcitability during GABA-A receptor downregulation and NMDA upregulation following chronic alcohol use.

results.finding: Alcohol withdrawal SE: high-dose benzodiazepines first-line - benzodiazepine receptor agonism corrects GABA-A downregulation
Phenobarbital addition: GABA-A positive allosteric modulator; additive with benzodiazepines for refractory withdrawal SE
Phenytoin NOT recommended for alcohol withdrawal SE - does not prevent withdrawal seizures
CIWA-Ar protocol after SE stabilized: symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing
Thiamine 500 mg IV TID x3-5 days for Wernicke encephalopathy treatment (Prescott protocol)

output.summary: Alcohol withdrawal seizures: benzodiazepines are first-line, correcting GABA-A downregulation. Phenobarbital provides additive benefit via GABA-A positive allosteric modulation for refractory withdrawal SE. Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures and is not recommended for this indication. Thiamine deficiency encephalopathy: high-dose IV thiamine (500 mg TID for 3–5 days) is standard treatment (Prescott protocol). Electrolyte repletion — potassium, magnesium, phosphate — is critical in alcohol-related withdrawal management. CIWA-Ar symptom-triggered protocols reduce total benzodiazepine exposure after initial stabilisation.

sequence_constraints.reason: Thiamine 500 mg IV must be given BEFORE any glucose in alcoholic patient with suspected Wernicke.

critical_actions: Administer IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg first-line for SE
Administer IV thiamine 500 mg TID for 3 days BEFORE any glucose — Wernicke prevention/treatment
Correct severe hypomagnesemia (Mg 0.8) — essential cofactor for thiamine
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT give IV glucose before thiamine in chronic alcoholic — precipitates Wernicke
Do NOT use phenytoin in cerebellar/Wernicke patients — worsens ataxia
Do NOT under-dose thiamine — 100 mg is prophylactic; treatment requires 500 mg TID
Do NOT administer IV glucose without first giving IV thiamine 500 mg in suspected Wernicke — risk of precipitating or worsening Wernicke encephalopathy.
key_reasoning_points: Chronic alcoholism causes thiamine deficiency; IV glucose alone can precipitate Wernicke by exhausting remaining thiamine
Thiamine 500 mg IV TID for at least 3 days is the treatment dose; 100 mg/day is prophylactic
Hypoglycemia + hypomagnesemia + thiamine deficiency form a triad that drives SE in alcoholics
Glucose administration is one of the SE workup steps requiring caveat in alcoholics
